result:
The first thing you learn when someone hands you a thousand words is how heavy they feel. Not heavy like stones, but heavy like keys. You think you can carry them easily until you actually try to put them in your pockets. I have a thousand keys now. Let's see which doors they open. The first door is always childhood. It smells like crayons and grass and the particular way sunlight fell across your kitchen floor at four in the afternoon. You don't remember being that small, but your body does. Somewhere deeper, it still remembers everything perfectly always quietly. 

My childhood kitchen had yellow wallpaper that I hated. It had little brown roosters on it, repeating forever, and I used to count them when I was bored. There were forty-three roosters on the wall facing the sink. I know because I counted them during the summer my parents fought about money every night. The roosters never fought. They just stood there, smug, holding their little pitchforks or whatever roosters hold. I wanted to peel them off one by one. Eventually I did, leaving tiny white scars where roosters had once been. I never told anyone. I still remember that 

The second door is adolescence, which smells like cheap body spray and anxiety. You get a hundred words for this part because you used a hundred different personas trying to figure out which one fit. I was the smart kid, then the quiet kid, then briefly, disastrously, the kid who tried to be funny in class and wasn't. You think adulthood will be about finding yourself. It's actually about realizing you were never really lost, you were just unfinished. Unfinished is not the same as broken, though it took me years to understand the difference and forgive the confusion anyway 

The third door is love. Not romantic love, at first. The love of a dog that waits for you to come home even though you left only five minutes ago to take out the trash. The love of a friend who texts you memes at midnight because they know you're still awake worrying. Then later, the other love. The one that makes your chest do that stupid painful hopeful thump. The one that makes you rewrite the same text message fourteen times. I wasted so many of my thousand words trying to say I love you without saying it directly 

Then comes the fourth door, which is work. We pretend it isn't a door but it is. It's the door you walk through every morning. For years I thought I needed to find meaningful work, work that would justify my existence in capital letters on a resume. Now I think work is just work. Some days it means something, some days it's just how you pay for electricity. Both are fine. I spent my twenties terrified of becoming mediocre. In my thirties I learned mediocre is just another word for human, and human is enough more than enough actually always 

The fifth door is grief, and you don't want to open it. But you have to because you have a thousand words and you cannot skip any doors. Grief smells like an empty closet and sounds like a phone that doesn't ring. When my grandfather died, I kept his old flannel shirt. I didn't wash it. I wore it until it didn't smell like him anymore, then I felt guilty for washing the last of him away. Grief is not linear. It's a messy apartment you keep meaning to clean but never do. Instead you learn living around it quietly 

The sixth door is the present moment, which is weird because it's always here but we rarely visit. Right now, as I write this, my coffee is getting cold. There's a fly bumping against the window. My neighbor is mowing his lawn. This is it. This is the life I was waiting for to start. I used to think there would be trumpets or some clear sign that adulthood had officially begun. There wasn't. There was just Tuesday afternoon, coffee, fly, lawnmower. If you are waiting for permission to start living, this is it. Consider yourself permissioned right here now. 

The seventh door is the future, which is blank and terrifying and therefore full of possibility. I used to be scared of getting old. Wrinkles, forgetting words, becoming irrelevant. Now I'm scared of not getting old. Of not getting the chance. My future self is somewhere ahead, waving me forward. I don't know if she's happy. I hope she has a dog. I hope she still laughs loudly. I hope she forgave me for mistakes I'm making today. If you meet her, tell her I'm trying. Tell her I'm trying hard with these thousand imperfect borrowed heavy keys today always 

The eighth door is imagination, which is where I've been all along. That's the trick of a thousand words. You start opening doors that aren't real, and suddenly you are home. Imagination smells like old libraries and ozone before rain. I used to think imagination was for children. Now I know adults need it more, because we have mortgages and dentist appointments and news cycles that never stop. My imagination is where I keep the rooster wallpaper, the cold coffee, the flannel shirt. It's where nothing is ever truly lost. It keeps everything safe until we need it again someday 

The ninth and tenth doors are the same door, because I am running out of keys. One door is you, reading this. One door is me, writing this. Between us, these thousand words are a bridge. I don't know your name. I don't know what your kitchen looked like. But you counted roosters with me for a while. You carried keys. That is enough to be called company. If you have words left after this, use them kindly. Write someone a letter. Tell the truth. Leave the roosters on the wall. They were never really bothering anyone anyway you know
